title: Watershed Finder: Which Basin Drains Your Point?
description: Find the watershed and drainage-basin context for any map point with the Watershed Finder — see which river system your rain joins. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a point on the Montana side of the Continental Divide sends its rain toward the Gulf of Mexico via the Missouri and Mississippi, while a point a ridge away sends its snowmelt to the Pacific.
quick_answer: The Watershed Finder shows the drainage context for a point on the map — the watershed whose streams carry its rain to one river system and one sea. Set a point and read which basin claims it: the invisible geography deciding where every raindrop eventually ends up.

Anglers and watershed groups organise by basin because fish and pollution do. Knowing which system your creek joins is the first fact of local water.
'The Colorado basin' in a headline is a place, roughly 640,000 km² (247,000 sq mi) of the published basin area. This finder shows whether a given town is inside the story.

The Mississippi River basin covers about 3.22 million km² (about 1.24 million sq mi) in published USGS figures — parts of 31 US states and two Canadian provinces. A click in Minnesota, Montana or Pennsylvania is usually inside it.

At Triple Divide Peak in Montana, three basins meet: rain can leave toward the Pacific, the Atlantic via the Gulf, or Hudson Bay. Watershed boundaries are the rare property lines drawn entirely by gravity.

faq: The land area that drains to a common outlet — a stream, river, lake or sea. The word covers both the boundary ridge and the territory inside it; North America says watershed, British usage often says catchment or drainage basin.

From elevation: water flows downhill, so divides follow ridgelines in terrain data. This finder's context derives from terrain-based drainage data — the same logic the Terrain Elevation Grid Map visualises locally.
Does a point near a divide always drain one way?
On the map, yes by elevation; in the field, karst limestone, drains, canals and flat wetlands can cheat. Treat flat and engineered landscapes as 'verify locally' country.
Why does my town name a different basin than my creek?
Basins nest. Your creek belongs to a small sub-basin, inside a river basin, inside a continental drainage. Different maps name different levels of the nest — both can be right.
Can groundwater cross a watershed line?
Yes — aquifers ignore surface divides, sometimes spectacularly in limestone country. Surface watershed and groundwater basin are cousins, not twins.
Is this the same as a flood zone?

No. A watershed says where water eventually goes; a flood zone says where water has been and may be again, from official hazard modelling. Never substitute one for the other in a purchase or insurance decision.

Constantly at the small scale — storm drains and grading move local runoff across natural divides. The named big-basin allegiance of a point rarely changes; the garden-scale path of its rain often does.
What about points in the ocean or a lake?
Open water is the bottom of someone else's watershed. The finder is a land tool; clicking the sea returns the sea.
